title: EditJudge-Bench: Auditing VLM Image-Edit Judges with Synthetic Ground Truth
claim: Procedurally editing controlled 3D scenes yields factual and counterfactual edit triplets that expose failures in automated judges.
layout: 2 rows by 3 columns, left-to-right arrows, factual top and counterfactual bottom
description: The figure has two horizontal rows on light gray backgrounds, read left to right with teal arrows between three columns labeled 3D Scene, Edit Triplet and Judge Evaluation. The left column shows Blender object renders (chair, shelf, wardrobe, lamp, plant) with xyz axes and a caption such as "*Rotates chair*" or "*Moves book up*". The middle column shows side-by-side Source and Edited rendered room images. The top row is labeled "Factual" and its instruction is "Rotate the chair". The bottom row is labeled "Counterfactual" in red and its instruction is "Move the books down", which contradicts the actual edit. The right column shows a cartoon robot judge holding a gavel and a thumbs-up or thumbs-down sign, with red FAIL stamps and quoted verdicts. The two verdicts are wrong: one calls identical images bad, the other approves the wrong direction. The eye goes first to the robot judges and the FAIL stamps.
caption: Auditing VLM image-edit judges with EDITJUDGE-BENCH. We procedurally alter 3D scenes (left) producing (source, edited, instruction) triplets (middle). We construct factual (top) and counterfactual (bottom) triplets to audit VLM image-edit judges (right), exposing reliability gaps in current VLM-as-a-judge evaluation protocols.
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for image-editing benchmarks, yet their reliability is poorly understood. Auditing these judges is difficult because real edited images lack controlled ground truth and entangle the requested changes with model artefacts, unintended side effects, and ambiguous degrees of success. In this paper, we introduce EditJudge-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,382 synthetic before/after image pairs rendered in Blender, with edits parameterised across nine categories derived from real user requests and exact ground truth from known 3D scene parameters. Because every edit is generated by a known intervention on a controlled scene, EditJudge-Bench evaluates VLM judges as binary verifiers of whether an instruction was correctly executed, isolating judge perception from editor quality. Across 25 judge configurations, we find substantial reliability gaps: (a) the widely adopted VIEScore template reaches only 69.0% AUROC with GPT-4o; (b) fine-tuned judges score 51.7-66.3%; spatial edits such as rotation and shape remain challenging; (c) prompt-formatting choices like image-text ordering shift performance by up to 14.1 points. Despite using only synthetic data, judge rankings on EditJudge-Bench correlate strongly with two real-image human-preference benchmarks ($Ï$=0.95 and $Ï$=0.71), indicating that controlled audits surface failure modes relevant to real evaluation.
